answer.question: My mom just turned 65 and is signing up for Medicare. How much will her Part B premium be each month in 2026, and is there anything that could make it higher?
answer.answer:
The standard Part B premium in 2026 is $202.90 a month, and most people pay that amount. Two things can make it higher:

1. **Higher income (IRMAA).** Medicare looks at the modified adjusted gross income on the IRS tax return from 2 years ago. For 2026, if her 2024 modified adjusted gross income was above $109,000 filing individually (or $218,000 married filing jointly), she may pay an extra charge called the Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA). You can learn more at Medicare.gov, and if she has to pay extra but disagrees (for example, her income is lower now because of a life event), visit SSA.gov/medicare/lower-irmaa.

2. **Late enrollment penalty.** If she doesn't sign up for Part B when first eligible, her monthly premium may go up 10% for each full 12 months she could have had Part B but didn't sign up, and she'd pay that for as long as she has Part B. (She may not owe the penalty if she signs up during a Special Enrollment Period or enrolls in a Medicare Savings Program.) Since she's signing up now at 65, during her Initial Enrollment Period, this penalty shouldn't apply.

If she has limited income and resources, pages 91–92 of the handbook describe programs that may help pay these costs. Note that a high income can also add an extra amount to a Part D drug coverage premium.

answer.question: Dad has Original Medicare and no other insurance. He spent 5 days in the hospital and then went straight into a skilled nursing facility for 30 days. What will he owe for that in 2026?
answer.answer:
Based on the handbook's 2026 Part A amounts, here's how it works out for a 5-day inpatient hospital stay followed by 30 days in a skilled nursing facility (SNF) in the same benefit period — a "benefit period" is the stretch of care measured from when he's admitted until he's been out of the hospital or SNF for 60 days in a row:

- Hospital: he pays the $1,736 Part A deductible for the benefit period; for days 1–60 in the hospital, after the deductible he pays $0 each day. So 5 days = $1,736.
- SNF: he does not pay the deductible again, because he already paid it for the hospital care in the same benefit period. Days 1–20 cost $0 each day, and days 21–100 cost $217 each day. Days 21–30 is 10 days × $217 = $2,170.

That's about $3,906 in Part A costs ($1,736 + $2,170). Note that if he also has Part B, Part B generally covers 80% of the Medicare‑approved amount for doctors' services he gets while in the hospital, so he'd owe his share of those separately. Also, Medicare only covers SNF care after a 3-day minimum medically necessary inpatient hospital stay (not counting the day he leaves the hospital) for an illness or injury related to the hospital stay, and his doctor must certify he needs daily skilled care.

For his exact bills, he can call 1-800-MEDICARE (TTY 1-877-486-2048) or visit Medicare.gov/coverage/skilled-nursing-facility-care.

answer.question: What are the 2026 income and resource limits for qualifying for Extra Help with Medicare drug costs?
answer.answer:
The handbook doesn't list the 2026 limits — it tells you to look them up: "You can find 2026 income and resource limits on Medicare.gov."

The figures printed in the handbook are the 2025 limits. You may qualify for Extra Help if your yearly income and resources are below these limits in 2025: a single person — yearly income less than $23,475 and resources less than $17,600; a married person living with a spouse and no other dependents — yearly income less than $31,725 and resources less than $35,130. In some situations you may qualify even with higher income, for example if you still work, live in Alaska or Hawaii, or have dependents living with you.

Resources include money in a checking or savings account, stocks, bonds, mutual funds, and IRAs. They don't include your home, car, household items, burial plot, up to $1,500 for burial expenses (per person), or life insurance policies.

For help, you can call your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) at shiphelp.org, or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227); TTY users can call 1-877-486-2048. You can apply any time at SSA.gov/extrahelp.

answer.answer:
No. Original Medicare doesn't cover hearing aids or the exams to fit them, so you'd pay the full cost yourself unless you have other coverage (like Medicaid) or are in a Medicare Advantage Plan or Medicare Cost Plan — those plans may cover extra benefits like hearing services.

Medicare does cover diagnostic hearing and balance (fall risk) exams if a doctor or health care provider orders them to see if medical treatment is needed. Your mother can also see an audiologist once every 12 months without an order, but only for non-acute hearing conditions (like hearing loss that develops over many years) and for diagnostic services related to hearing loss treated with surgically implanted hearing devices. For those exams she pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount, the Part B deductible applies, and there's also a copayment in a hospital outpatient setting.

answer.question: I'm 68 and still working at a company with 12 employees, and I have the company health plan as well as Medicare. Which one pays my medical bills first?
answer.answer:
Because you're 65 or older with group health plan coverage from your current job at an employer with fewer than 20 employees, Medicare generally pays first, and your company plan pays second. One exception: if your small employer's plan is part of a multi-employer plan that includes other employers with 20 or more employees, the group health plan pays first.

Keep in mind the payer that pays first (the "primary payer") pays up to the limits of its coverage, and the second payer only pays costs the first didn't cover — and may not pay all of them. Since your situation depends on your employer's plan, contact your employer to find out how its coverage works with Medicare. You can also read "How Medicare Works with Other Insurance" at Medicare.gov/health-drug-plans/coordination or Medicare.gov/publications, or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227); TTY users can call 1-877-486-2048.

answer.question: My mom turns 65 on March 12. When can she sign up for Medicare without paying a penalty, and when would her coverage start?
answer.answer:
Because her birthday (March 12) isn't on the first of the month, her Initial Enrollment Period is the 7-month window that begins 3 months before the month she turns 65 and ends 3 months after — so December through June, with March being her birthday month. Signing up in that window avoids a late enrollment penalty.

When coverage starts depends on when she signs up:
- If she signs up during the first 3 months (December, January, or February), in most cases her coverage begins the first day of her birthday month — March 1.
- If she signs up in March (the month she turns 65) or during the last 3 months (April, May, or June), her coverage starts the first day of the month after she signs up.

Note: if she's already getting Social Security or Railroad Retirement Board benefits, she'll get Part A and Part B automatically starting the first day of the month she turns 65. If she isn't getting those benefits, she needs to sign up — she can apply at SSA.gov/medicare/sign-up or contact Social Security 3 months before she turns 65 to set up an appointment.

answer.question: My husband is retiring in April and I'm 67 and covered by his employer's health plan. How long will I have to sign up for Part B, and does taking COBRA buy me more time?
answer.answer: Because you're covered by a group health plan based on your husband's current employment, you get a Special Enrollment Period: you can sign up for Part B any time while you're still covered by that plan, and then during the 8-month period that begins the month after the employment ends or the coverage ends, whichever happens first. Usually you won't owe a late enrollment penalty if you sign up in that window. Taking COBRA does not buy you more time. COBRA isn't considered coverage based on current employment, so it doesn't count for this Special Enrollment Period — after coverage based on current employment ends you have 8 months to sign up for Part B without a penalty, whether or not you choose COBRA, and you generally aren't eligible for a Special Enrollment Period when the COBRA coverage ends. The handbook also warns that if you have COBRA and you're eligible for Medicare, COBRA may only pay a small portion of your medical costs. To sign up, visit SSA.gov/medicare/sign-up; if you're unsure whether you qualify for an enrollment period, visit Medicare.gov or call 1-800-MEDICARE.

answer.question: Mom has Original Medicare and nothing else. Is there a cap on what she can be charged out of pocket in a year, and would a Medicare Advantage plan cap it?
answer.answer:
No. With Original Medicare by itself, there's no yearly limit on what she pays out of pocket — she pays the Part A and Part B deductibles (the Part B deductible is $283 in 2026), then coinsurance or copayments, usually 20% of the Medicare-approved amount for Part B services. Limits only apply if she has supplemental coverage like Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap), Medicaid, or employer, retiree, or union coverage.

A Medicare Advantage (Part C) plan does cap it: plans have a yearly limit on what you pay for covered Medicare services (which may include different limits for in-network and out-of-network services), and once she reaches the plan's limit, she pays nothing for covered services for the rest of the year. Out-of-pocket costs and the limit amounts vary by plan, so she'd need to check a specific plan's details.

answer.question: My mother found a Medicare Advantage plan with a $0 monthly premium. Does that mean she would pay nothing each month for her Medicare?
answer.answer:
No. A $0 plan premium only means the plan itself doesn't charge a monthly premium — she would still usually pay her Part B premium (and a Part A premium if she doesn't have premium-free Part A). The handbook says: "Some Medicare Advantage Plans have a $0 premium (but you still may pay the Part B premium)." Some Medicare Advantage Plans do help pay all or part of the Part B premium, sometimes called a "Medicare Part B premium reduction," so it's worth checking whether her plan does that.

Two other things that could add to her monthly cost: most people don't pay a Part A premium if they or their spouse paid Medicare taxes long enough while working, but if she has to buy Part A, it costs $311 or $565 each month in 2026. And if her income is above a certain limit (in 2026, $109,000 filing individually or $218,000 married filing jointly), she'd pay an extra amount for drug coverage — "Part D IRMAA" — even in a Medicare Advantage plan that includes drug coverage. A $0 premium also doesn't mean $0 for care; she may still owe copayments and deductibles when she uses services.

answer.question: My father takes several expensive prescriptions. Is there any cap on what he'll have to pay for his drugs in 2026?
answer.answer:
Yes. If your father has Medicare drug coverage (Part D), his yearly out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered by his plan are capped at $2,100 in 2026. Once he reaches that limit — counting his own out-of-pocket spending plus certain payments others make on his behalf, including Medicare's Extra Help program — he won't pay a copayment or coinsurance for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year.

A few things to know: the cap applies only to drugs covered by his plan (on the plan's list of covered drugs, or formulary), and it doesn't cover his monthly plan premium. What he pays before reaching the cap depends on his plan's deductible, the "tier" his drugs are in, and which pharmacy he uses.

He may also be able to spread those out-of-pocket costs across the year (January–December) through the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan — though that doesn't lower his total drug costs. If he has a limited income, Extra Help may reduce some of these Part D costs. For specific plan costs, visit Medicare.gov/plan-compare or call his State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP).

answer.question: Dad is 68, has had Medicare since he was 65 and never joined a drug plan because he takes no medication. If he joins one now, will he be charged a penalty, and how is it worked out?
answer.answer:
Yes — most likely he'll owe a late enrollment penalty. The handbook says you may have to pay the penalty if you enroll any time after your Initial Enrollment Period is over and you go 63 or more days in a row without Medicare drug coverage or other "creditable" prescription drug coverage (drug coverage at least as good as Medicare's, such as from a current or former employer or union, TRICARE, the Indian Health Service, or the VA). Taking no medication doesn't excuse it — the handbook says that even if you don't take drugs now, you should consider joining a plan to avoid a penalty.

How it's worked out: 1% of the "national base beneficiary premium" ($38.99 in 2026) is multiplied by the number of full, uncovered months he was eligible but had no Medicare drug coverage or other creditable coverage. The result is rounded to the nearest $.10 and added to his monthly plan premium, generally for as long as he has Medicare drug coverage. The base premium can change each year, so the penalty amount can go up or down. After he joins, the plan will tell him if he owes a penalty and what his premium will be. If he gets Extra Help, he doesn't pay a late enrollment penalty. If he disagrees with the penalty, the plan's letter comes with a "reconsideration request form," and he can ask for a review (generally within 60 days from the date on the letter).

One thing to check: if he has had creditable drug coverage all along (for example from an employer or the VA), he may owe nothing — but he should keep records of it and tell the plan when asked, or he may be charged a penalty for as long as he has the coverage.

answer.question: Dad is comparing Medigap Plan K and Plan L. What is the most each one would let him pay out of pocket in 2026, and how much of his costs do they cover?
answer.answer: In 2026, Plan K has an out-of-pocket yearly limit of $8,000 and Plan L has a limit of $4,000. Until he reaches that limit, Plan K pays 50% and Plan L pays 75% of these benefits: Medicare Part B coinsurance or copayment, the blood benefit (first 3 pints), Part A hospice care coinsurance or copayment, skilled nursing facility care coinsurance, and the Part A deductible. Both plans pay 100% of Medicare Part A coinsurance and hospital costs (up to an additional 365 days after Medicare benefits are used). Neither covers the Part B deductible, Part B excess charges, or foreign travel emergency care. Once he meets the out-of-pocket yearly limit and his yearly Part B deductible ($283 in 2026), the Medigap plan pays 100% of covered services for the rest of the calendar year. Keep in mind the monthly premium is separate — he pays it to the private insurance company in addition to his monthly Part B premium, and costs can vary between companies for the same coverage.

answer.question: When is the best time for my dad to buy a Medigap policy, and what happens if he waits?
answer.answer: The best time is during his Medigap Open Enrollment Period — a 6-month period that begins the first month he has Medicare Part B (Medical Insurance) and he's 65 or older. (Some states have additional Open Enrollment Periods.) If he waits until after that period, he may not be able to buy a Medigap policy at all, or it may cost more. In certain situations he may still have the right to buy a policy outside that period (called guaranteed issue rights). Note: if he's delaying Part B because he has group health coverage based on his or his spouse's current employment, his Medigap Open Enrollment Period won't start until he gets Part B. To learn more about his rights to buy a Medigap policy, he can call his State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) (phone numbers on pages 114–117) or his State Insurance Department, or visit Medicare.gov/medigap-supplemental-insurance-plans to find policies and pricing in his area.

answer.question: Dad signed up for Part B this past January. His doctor's office wants to book him for his annual wellness visit. Is he eligible for that yet, and what will it cost him?
answer.answer:
Not yet. The yearly “Wellness” visit is only for people who have had Part B for longer than 12 months, and your dad's first one can't take place within 12 months of his Part B enrollment (or of a “Welcome to Medicare” preventive visit). Since his Part B began this past January, he'd need to wait until more than 12 months after that enrollment.

In the meantime, during his first 12 months with Part B he can get a one-time “Welcome to Medicare” preventive visit — it isn't a physical exam, but a review of his medical and social history plus education, counseling about preventive services, and referrals if needed. Tell the doctor's office that's what he'd like to schedule.

Cost: he pays nothing for either the “Welcome to Medicare” preventive visit or the yearly “Wellness” visit if the doctor or other provider accepts assignment (agrees to the Medicare-approved amount). But if the provider does extra tests or services during the visit that Medicare doesn't cover under the preventive benefit, he may owe coinsurance and the Part B deductible may apply; for things Medicare doesn't cover at all (like a routine physical exam), he may have to pay the full amount.

answer.question: Mom's doctor wants to set up home health care after her hip surgery. What will Medicare charge her for it, and does she have to be bedridden to qualify?
answer.answer:
Cost: you pay nothing for covered home health services. The one exception is durable medical equipment (things like a walker or wheelchair) supplied through the benefit — for that you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount, and the Part B deductible applies.

She doesn't have to be bedridden. She has to be "homebound," which the handbook describes as: she has trouble leaving home without help (a cane, wheelchair, walker, crutches, special transportation, or another person) because of an illness or injury; or leaving home isn't recommended because of her condition; or she's normally unable to leave home because it's a major effort. She also must need part-time or intermittent skilled services — skilled nursing care and home health aide services up to 8 hours a day (combined), for a maximum of 28 hours each week (or up to 35 hours a week in some limited situations).

Also required: a doctor or other health care provider (like a nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant) must assess her face-to-face before certifying that she needs home health services, a doctor or other provider must order the care, and a Medicare-certified home health agency must provide it.

answer.question: Mom's cancer is terminal and her doctor brought up hospice. Who has to sign off before Medicare will cover it, and what would she have to pay?
answer.answer:
To qualify for hospice care, a hospice doctor and your mom's own doctor (if she has one) must certify that she's terminally ill, meaning a life expectancy of 6 months or less. She also has to sign a statement choosing hospice care (comfort care, also called palliative care) instead of other Medicare-covered treatments meant to cure her terminal illness and related conditions.

What she'd pay: nothing for hospice care itself; a copayment of up to $5 per prescription for outpatient drugs for pain and symptom management; and 5% of the Medicare-approved amount for inpatient respite care (a stay of up to 5 days at a time in a Medicare-approved facility so a caregiver can rest). Medicare won't pay room and board where she lives unless the hospice medical team decides she needs short-term inpatient care to manage pain and symptoms.

Hospice is billed to Original Medicare even if she's in a Medicare Advantage Plan, and she doesn't have to switch back to Original Medicare for it to be covered. For more on hospice care and to find Medicare-approved providers, she can contact her plan or visit Medicare.gov/care-compare.

answer.question: My parents have Original Medicare. They're going to Portugal in June and to Puerto Rico in October. Would Medicare cover them if one of them ended up in the hospital on either trip?
answer.answer:
The two trips are treated differently.

Portugal: Original Medicare generally doesn't cover medical care outside the U.S., so a hospital stay there generally wouldn't be covered. The handbook notes you may be able to buy a Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap) policy that covers emergency care outside the U.S.

Puerto Rico: With Original Medicare you can go to any Medicare-enrolled doctor, other health care provider, hospital, or other facility that accepts Medicare patients anywhere in the U.S. The excerpts list Puerto Rico among the U.S. territories, so care there is not the "outside the U.S." situation — though the excerpts don't spell out Puerto Rico hospital coverage in so many words. Normal Original Medicare cost sharing would apply, and there's no limit to what you'll pay out of pocket in a year unless you have other coverage (like Medigap, Medicaid, employer, retiree, or union coverage).

For certainty about a specific trip or hospital, they can call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227); TTY users can call 1-877-486-2048, or check Medicare.gov/care-compare for providers that accept Medicare.

answer.question: Mom spent three nights in the hospital but the billing office says she was under observation the whole time, never admitted. She needs a skilled nursing facility now. Will Part A pay for it?
answer.answer:
Most likely not. Part A covers short-term skilled nursing facility (SNF) care only after a 3-day minimum medically necessary **inpatient** hospital stay (not counting the day she leaves) for an illness or injury related to that stay. Time spent getting observation services counts as outpatient care, even if she spent nights in the hospital — you're an inpatient only when the hospital formally admits you with a doctor's order. So observation nights don't meet the 3-day inpatient requirement.

Two things worth checking:
- If she was under observation more than 24 hours, the hospital must give her a "Medicare Outpatient Observation Notice" ("MOON") explaining why she's an outpatient and how it affects what she pays for care after she leaves. If the hospital changed her status from inpatient to outpatient, she now has appeal rights if she meets certain conditions (see page 101 or Medicare.gov/providers-services/claims-appeals-complaints/appeals/original-medicare).
- The 3-day stay can sometimes be waived: she may not need it if her doctor participates in an Accountable Care Organization (ACO) approved for a Skilled Nursing Facility 3-Day Rule Waiver, and Medicare Advantage Plans may also waive the 3-day minimum — ask the provider or the plan.

If SNF care is covered under a benefit period, she'd pay $1,736 first, then $0 a day for days 1–20, $217 each day for days 21–100, and all costs from day 101 on.

answer.question: My father moved to the U.S. at 58 and has only about 6 years of work here. Does he have to pay for Part A, how much in 2026, and what happens if he puts it off?
answer.answer:
The handbook explains the general rule, though it doesn't spell out how many years of work are needed. You usually pay no monthly Part A (hospital insurance) premium if you or your spouse paid Medicare taxes while working for a certain amount of time — this is called "premium-free Part A." If your father isn't eligible for premium-free Part A, he may be able to buy it: in 2026 the premium is either $311 or $565 each month, depending on how long he or his spouse worked and paid Medicare taxes. In most cases, if he buys Part A he must also have Part B and pay monthly premiums for both; if he chooses not to buy Part A, he can still buy Part B if he's eligible.

If he's not eligible for premium-free Part A and doesn't buy it when first eligible, his monthly premium may go up 10%, and he'd pay the higher premium for twice the number of years he could have had Part A but didn't sign up (for example, 2 years without signing up means 4 years of the 10% higher premium).

If he needs help paying the Part A premium, see pages 91–92. For questions about paying for Part A, visit Medicare.gov or call 1-800-MEDICARE. Whether his 6 years of U.S. work qualify him for premium-free Part A isn't stated in these excerpts — Social Security can confirm that.

answer.question: Mom's only income is her Social Security check and she's struggling to pay her Medicare premiums. Is there a program that would help, and would it do anything for her drug costs?
answer.answer:
Yes — two programs, and they connect to each other.

**Medicare Savings Programs** are state-run programs that help pay Medicare costs like premiums. In most cases your income and resources must be below a certain limit, and those limits vary by state — but the handbook says that even if you don't think you qualify, you should still apply. To start, contact your State Medical Assistance (Medicaid) office; you can get your state's number at Medicaid.gov/about-us/where-can-people-get-help-medicaid-chip or by calling 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227), TTY 1-877-486-2048. (These programs aren't available in Puerto Rico or the U.S. Virgin Islands.)

**For drug costs: Extra Help.** If your mom qualifies for a QMB, SLMB, or QI Program (the Medicare Savings Programs), she qualifies automatically for Extra Help, which helps pay some Medicare drug costs like premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance. She also won't pay a Part D late enrollment penalty if she qualifies for Extra Help and joins a Medicare drug plan or a Medicare Advantage Plan with drug coverage.

If she doesn't qualify automatically, she can apply for Extra Help any time at SSA.gov/extrahelp — and that application can also begin the Medicare Savings Program application process, since Social Security will send information to her state unless she tells them not to.

The 2025 Extra Help limits were yearly income less than $23,475 and resources less than $17,600 for a single person; 2026 income and resource limits are on Medicare.gov. Resources include checking/savings, stocks, bonds, mutual funds and IRAs, but not her home, car, household items, burial plot, up to $1,500 for burial expenses, or life insurance.

For free help with questions about Extra Help or choosing drug coverage, she can call her State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) — see pages 114–117 or shiphelp.org.

In most cases that copayment can't be more than the Part A hospital stay deductible for each service (the Part A deductible is $1,736 in 2026), and the Part B deductible applies. If the hospital is a critical access hospital (a small rural facility), the copayment may be higher and may exceed the Part A deductible. answer.question: Mom is in a Medicare Advantage plan and wants to move to a different one for next year. When can she make that change, and when would the new plan kick in?
answer.answer:
She can switch during the Open Enrollment Period, October 15 to December 7. If the new plan gets her enrollment request by December 7, her new coverage starts January 1.

If she changes her mind later, she also has the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period, January 1 to March 31, when someone already in a Medicare Advantage Plan can switch to another Medicare Advantage Plan (with or without drug coverage). She can only switch once during that period, and the new coverage starts the first of the month after the plan gets her request.

Outside those windows she generally can't change plans during the year, unless she qualifies for a Special Enrollment Period — for example, if she moves or loses other insurance coverage — or if a plan with a 5-star quality rating is available to her.

answer.question: Mom joined a Medicare Advantage plan in January and already regrets it. It's now February. Can she move to a different plan, and how many times can she change?
answer.answer: Yes — February falls inside the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period, when someone already in a Medicare Advantage Plan can switch to a different Medicare Advantage Plan or go back to Original Medicare (and join a separate Medicare drug plan). But she can only make one change during this period, and the change takes effect the first of the month after the plan gets her request. If she returns to Original Medicare and joins a separate drug plan, she doesn't need to contact her Medicare Advantage Plan to disenroll — that happens automatically. After that one change, she generally has to keep the plan for the rest of the year unless she qualifies for a Special Enrollment Period (for example, if she moves or loses other insurance coverage), or unless a 5-star plan is available in her area — the 5-star Special Enrollment Period also allows only one switch. For help, she can call her State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP); the phone number is on pages 114–117.

answer.question: Mom sees a cardiologist regularly and has a stress test every year. If she moves from Original Medicare to a Medicare Advantage plan, will she suddenly need referrals and pre-approvals she doesn't need now?
answer.answer: Possibly, yes — it depends on the plan she picks. With Original Medicare, "you don’t need a referral to use a specialist in most cases, and you generally don’t need prior approval to use a covered benefit." Each Medicare Advantage Plan, though, sets its own rules for how you get services — including whether you need a referral to see a specialist and whether you must use doctors, facilities, and suppliers in the plan's network for non-emergency or non-urgent care — and those rules can change each year, with the plan notifying you before the next enrollment year starts. The handbook says it's important to follow the plan's rules, like getting prior approval for a certain service when needed, and that if you go outside the network without authorization you may have to pay the full cost. So before switching, she should check the specific plan's "Evidence of Coverage," which gives details about what the plan covers and how much she pays. One exception the handbook names: a Medicare Medical Savings Account (MSA) Plan doesn't require choosing a primary care doctor or a referral to see a specialist. Also note that if a plan's network changes and a provider she has seen in the past three years leaves, the plan must notify her, help her choose a new provider, and help her continue needed care that's already in progress; and when an in-network provider can't meet her medical needs, the plan must help her get medically necessary covered services outside the network at in-network cost sharing.

answer.question: Mom is down to two Medicare Advantage plans, an HMO and a PPO. Would she have to pick a primary care doctor or get referrals, and what happens if she sees a doctor outside the network?
answer.answer:
The two plan types work differently:

**HMO.** In most cases, yes — she'd need to choose a primary care doctor, and in most cases she'd need a referral to see a specialist (some services, like yearly mammogram screenings, don't require a referral). She generally must get care from doctors, other providers, or hospitals in the plan's network, except for emergency care, out-of-area urgent care, or temporary out-of-area dialysis. Some HMOs, called HMO Point-of-Service (HMOPOS) Plans, may let her get some out-of-network services for a higher copayment or coinsurance. "If you get non-emergency health care outside the plan's network without authorization, you may have to pay the full cost."

**PPO.** She doesn't have to choose a primary care doctor, and in most cases doesn't need a referral for a specialist. A PPO has network providers, but she can also use out-of-network providers for covered services, usually for a higher cost, if the provider agrees to treat her and hasn't opted out of Medicare (for Part A and Part B items and services). Emergency and urgent care are always covered. Using in-network ("preferred") specialists usually costs less.

For details on either specific plan, check with the plan or visit Medicare.gov.

answer.answer:
Yes. If her income is above the limit (in 2026, $109,000 filing individually or $218,000 married filing jointly), she pays an extra amount on top of her plan premium — sometimes called "Part D IRMAA" — and the handbook says this applies too if she's in a Medicare Advantage Plan that includes drug coverage.

She does not pay it to the plan. Usually Medicare or the Railroad Retirement Board (RRB) deducts the extra amount from her Social Security or RRB payment. If Medicare or the RRB bills her instead, she must pay the extra amount to Medicare or the RRB, not her plan. If she doesn't pay it, she could lose her Medicare drug coverage (Part D), may not be able to join another plan right away, and may owe a late enrollment penalty for as long as she has drug coverage. The extra amount is paid separately even if an employer or another third party pays her plan premiums. If she has to pay Part D IRMAA and disagrees (for example, she has one or more life-changing events that lower her income), she can visit SSA.gov/medicare/lower-irmaa.

answer.question: Mom takes insulin every day. Is there a limit on what her Medicare drug plan can charge her for it, and does she have to meet her deductible first?
answer.answer:
Yes. Under Medicare drug coverage (Part D), the cost of a one-month supply of each covered insulin product is capped at $35. The handbook excerpts you have say this cap applies to insulin you inject yourself that your drug plan covers, and similar caps apply to traditional insulin used in Part B-covered insulin pumps.

The excerpts don't state whether the deductible has to be met first for insulin. They explain generally that a plan's yearly deductible is the amount you pay before the plan pays its share, that some plans have no deductible, and that in some plans with a deductible, drugs on some tiers are covered before the deductible. Since drug plans differ, check with your mom's plan for how her insulin is handled, or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227); TTY users can call 1-877-486-2048.

One more cost note: in 2026 her out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered by her plan are capped at $2,100, and after she reaches that cap she pays no copayment or coinsurance for covered Part D drugs for the rest of the calendar year.

answer.question: Dad's drug plan puts his medicine on an expensive tier and his doctor says the cheaper ones won't work for him. Can he ask the plan to charge him less, and how does that work?
answer.answer:
Yes. This is called asking for an "exception" (a request that the plan make a change for your dad's specific situation). If his drug is on a higher tier and his prescriber — his doctor or other provider legally allowed to write prescriptions — thinks he needs that drug instead of a similar drug on a lower tier, your dad or his prescriber can ask the plan for an exception to get a lower coinsurance or copayment for the higher tier drug. He can ask if he or his prescriber believe he can't take any of the lower tier drugs for the same condition.

How it works: your dad or his prescriber must contact the plan to ask for the coverage determination or exception. For a prescription he hasn't gotten yet, either of them can make a standard request or an expedited (fast) request by phone or in writing; the request will be expedited if he hasn't gotten the prescription and the plan determines, or his prescriber tells the plan, that his life or health may be at risk by waiting. To be paid back for drugs he already bought, the plan can require the standard request in writing (an expedited request can be made by calling or writing the plan). If a network pharmacy can't fill the prescription, the pharmacist gives a notice explaining how to contact the plan to make the request — ask for a copy if it isn't given. The excerpts note the handbook has more on exceptions on page 100, and more information is at Medicare.gov/providers-services/claims-appeals-complaints/appeals/drug-plans.

**Plan N** — Plan N pays 100% of the Part B coinsurance, but you must pay a copayment of up to $20 for some office visits and up to a $50 copayment for emergency room visits that don't result in an inpatient admission. **High-deductible Plan G** — Plans F and G also offer a high-deductible version in some states. With it, you must pay Medicare-covered costs (coinsurance, copayments, and deductibles) up to the deductible amount of $2,950 in 2026 before your policy pays anything. Plan G also doesn't cover the Part B deductible.

answer.question: Dad has had a Medigap policy for years but wants to try a Medicare Advantage plan. If he hates it, can he get his Medigap policy back?
answer.answer:
Maybe — but only under limited "trial right" rules, so this is worth checking before he drops the Medigap policy.

If he drops a Medigap policy to join a Medicare Advantage Plan for the first time, he gets a single 12-month period (his "trial right period") to get his Medigap policy back — if the same insurance company still sells it once he returns to Original Medicare. If that policy isn't available, he can buy certain Medigap policies, depending on state law and whether he was new to Medicare on or after January 1, 2020. He may also have a chance to join a Medicare drug plan at that time. Some states provide additional special rights to buy a Medigap policy.

Outside that trial right period, the handbook warns he may not be able to get the same policy back, or in some cases any Medigap policy. Also note: most Medigap policies don't automatically cancel when you join a Medicare Advantage Plan, so he must contact his insurance company if he wants to cancel — and he can't use Medigap to pay his Medicare Advantage Plan copayments, deductibles, and premiums. Generally he can drop the Medicare Advantage Plan and return to Original Medicare within the first 12 months of joining, or during an enrollment period.

For help with his specific situation, he can call his State Insurance Department (content.naic.org/state-insurance-departments), his State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP), or visit Medicare.gov/medigap-supplemental-insurance-plans.

answer.question: How much would a Medigap Plan G policy cost my dad per month?
answer.answer:
The handbook doesn't list a monthly price for Plan G (or any Medigap plan). Medigap policies are sold by private insurance companies, and you pay a monthly premium to the company in addition to your monthly Part B premium. The handbook notes that "The costs can vary between plans offered by different companies for exactly the same coverage, and may go up as you get older," and that some states limit Medigap premium costs — so your dad's price depends on the company, his age, and his state.

To find actual prices, visit Medicare.gov/medigap-supplemental-insurance-plans to find policies and pricing in your area, call your State Insurance Department (get the number at content.naic.org/state-insurance-departments), or call your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP). One figure the handbook does give: if he chooses the high-deductible version of Plan G (offered in some states), he must pay Medicare-covered costs up to the deductible amount of $2,950 in 2026 before the policy pays anything.
